newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe launches political charm offensive.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe launches political charm offensive.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, under fire for his government's austerity policies in face of a weak economy and high unemployment, on Tuesday arranged a series of meetings aimed at rallying his fractious centre-right coalition.
Juppe's office announced a string of get-togethers arranged by the premier over the next few days with key political figures from the two ruling parties.

The meetings follow close on the heels of a similar round of political fence-mending by President Jacques Chirac in late July and early August. Chirac held talks with leaders from both the opposition and the coalition over a series of lunches.

The Gaullist Juppe's initiative, apparently aimed at rallying the fractious ruling bloc well ahead of a 1998 general election, coincided with the annual "rentree", the traditional return to work and school after the summer holidays.

This year's return has been marked by widespread gloom over persistent near-record unemployment and threatened social unrest over government plans to slash public deficits in order to help qualify for European monetary union from 1999.
The uncertain outlook has prompted a new wave of criticism of government policies from within its own ranks.
Among those being courted by Juppe were several members of the coalition who have taken aim at his economic policies in the past few days.

These include Gaullist National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, deputy Alain Madelin of the centrist Union for French Democracy (UDF) who was sacked last year as Juppe's finance minister, and UDF chief Francois Leotard.

Also on Juppe's meeting list were centrist Senate speaker Rene Monory, former UDF leader and ex-French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, Gaullist ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur, Gaullist ex-interior minister Charles Pasqua and current Education Minister Francois Bayrou, who is president of the centrist Democratic Force.
The charm offensive got off to a fortuitous start on Tuesday when UDF member Raymond Barre left a lunch with Juppe to proclaim that the prime minister's policies were "in line with reality".

"I hope the French people understand that we cannot return to the past, when we often pursued a policy of growth at any cost, only to find it led to a deterioration of our public finances, our currency and the competitiveness of our businesses," Barre said.
